blocks.text: Chat model fine-tuning extends instruction following, covered in the previous topic, from single-turn instruction and response pairs to full multi-turn conversations, where earlier exchanges shape how later turns should be interpreted and responded to.

This topic covers the conversational data format chat models train on, how loss masking works across a multi-turn exchange, and the practical considerations that come specifically from conversation history rather than isolated instructions.
1. Single Turn vs Multi Turn Training Data

blocks.alt: Single Turn vs Multi Turn Training Data
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472614889-850218356.png

Instruction following, covered in the previous topic, typically trains on isolated instruction and response pairs, chat model fine-tuning instead trains on full conversation sequences, where a model response needs to account for everything said earlier in the same conversation.
2. The Role-Based Message Structure
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472614890-686830514.png

Chat training data is organized around distinct roles, a system message setting overall behavior, alternating user and assistant messages representing the actual back and forth, a structure that lets the model learn to distinguish instructions from the system, input from the user, and its own prior responses.

code.content:
[
  {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful, concise assistant."},
  {"role": "user", "content": "What is the capital of France?"},
  {"role": "assistant", "content": "Paris."},
  {"role": "user", "content": "And its population?"},
  {"role": "assistant", "content": "About 2.1 million in the city proper."}
]

blocks.text: 3. Chat Templates
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472614890-715301365.png

Since a language model ultimately still processes a flat sequence of tokens, a chat template defines exactly how the role-structured conversation gets converted into a specific tagged text format the model is trained and later run with, using the wrong template at inference time, one that does not match what training used, silently produces degraded results.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Concept","What It Does"],"rows":[["Role structure","Organizes a conversation into system, user, assistant turns"],["Chat template","Converts that structure into the exact text format the model expects"]]}

blocks.text: 4. Context Carrying Across Turns
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472614891-671579087.png

A defining feature of multi-turn training data is that later assistant responses need to correctly reference or build on earlier context, "its population" in the example above only makes sense given the earlier mention of France, training data needs enough genuinely multi-turn examples to teach this context-carrying behavior specifically.
5. Loss Masking: Training Only on Assistant Turns

blocks.alt: Loss Masking: Training Only on Assistant Turns
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472614891-710892875.png

A common and important practice is masking the loss so it is only computed on the assistant response tokens, not on the system or user message tokens, since the model job is to generate good assistant responses, not to learn to predict what a user might say next.

blocks.title: Loss masking is an easy detail to get wrong
blocks.content: Training loss on user turns as well as assistant turns can subtly degrade quality, since the model ends up partially optimized toward predicting user behavior rather than purely toward producing good assistant responses.

blocks.text: 6. System Prompts and Persona Consistency
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472614892-790194491.png

Including varied system prompts in training data, different personas, tones, or constraints, teaches the model to consistently follow whatever system instruction it is given across an entire conversation, not just at the first turn, a real difference from single-turn instruction tuning where there is no ongoing behavior to sustain.
7. Context Window Limits in Practice
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472615222-834881862.png

Long conversations eventually exceed a model context window, covered in an earlier module, training data that includes some genuinely long conversations helps a model handle this gracefully, whether through summarizing earlier context or gracefully truncating, rather than only ever seeing short conversations during training.
8. Chat Models vs Retrieval Augmented Chat

Chat model fine-tuning as covered here focuses on the conversational format and turn-taking behavior itself, a chat model can separately be combined with retrieval augmented generation, covered in an earlier course, to ground its responses in external documents, the two concerns, conversational structure and factual grounding, are largely independent.
9. Evaluating Chat Model Quality

Evaluating chat models benefits from testing genuinely multi-turn scenarios, not just isolated single-turn quality, checking whether the model correctly tracks context, maintains persona consistency from the system prompt, and handles topic shifts within a conversation reasonably.
Worked Example

A team fine-tuning a customer support chat model builds training data from real multi-turn support conversations, masking loss to only the assistant turns and including a consistent system prompt describing the assistant role and tone.

During evaluation, they specifically test multi-turn scenarios where a user question late in the conversation depends on something mentioned several turns earlier, confirming the model correctly tracks that context rather than only evaluating isolated single-turn responses.
Common Mistakes

items: Training loss on user message tokens instead of masking to assistant turns only
Using a chat template at inference time that does not match the one used during training
Only training on short conversations, leaving the model poorly prepared for longer, context-heavy exchanges
Evaluating only single-turn quality and never testing whether context actually carries correctly across turns

blocks.text: Practice

Write a four-turn conversation example, system, user, assistant, user, assistant, where the second assistant response depends on information from the first user turn, then identify exactly which tokens in your example the training loss should and should not be computed on.
Key Takeaway

Chat model fine-tuning extends instruction following to full multi-turn conversations using a role-based data structure and a matching chat template, with loss masked to assistant turns only, and success depends specifically on the model correctly carrying context across turns and consistently following its system prompt throughout a conversation, not just producing good isolated responses.
